t: The Signature Ground-Grid Mat: Zoned Dissipative Layout
title: The Signature Ground-Grid Mat: Zoned Dissipative Layout
description: The Signature Ground-Grid Mat is Justin Addam Higgins' original ESD bench design: a 24x36 two-layer dissipative mat printed with a grounded zone grid — a CPU zone, a RAM zone, a GPU rest zone, and a tool zone — each zone bonded to the common ground through its own trace. Parts live in their zones, tools in theirs, and the grid makes 'parts on the mat' automatic because every part has a printed home. It is an ESD mat and a layout map in one.

demo.program:
zones = ["CPU zone (center)", "RAM zone (left)", "GPU rest zone (right)",
         "tool zone (top edge)", "screw zone (bottom edge)"]
print("Ground-Grid Mat zones (each bonded to common ground):")
for z in zones:
    print(f"  - {z}")

t: Signature Zone Bonding: One Ground, Many Printed Traces
title: Signature Zone Bonding: One Ground, Many Printed Traces
description: Under the printed grid, conductive traces run from each zone to the mat's ground snap, so every zone is verifiably at the same potential — no floating islands. The traces are part of the mat's conductive underlayer, not glued wires, so they cannot peel or snag. A single snap at the back feeds the common point ground. The design keeps the single-path rule while giving each zone its own visible home.

demo.program:
print("Zone -> trace -> single snap -> common point -> earth")
print("Traces are IN the conductive underlayer (no glued wires to fail).")
print("Result: every printed zone at equal potential, one ground path.")

t: Signature Wrist Strap: Dual-Band With Contact Indicator
title: Signature Wrist Strap: Dual-Band With Contact Indicator
description: The Signature strap uses a wide dual-band — conductive fabric plus a metal contact plate — that keeps skin contact even when your wrist flexes during cooler installs. A tiny continuity LED in the snap blinks green while the skin-to-ground path is intact and goes dark the moment contact breaks. It does not replace a tester, but it catches the classic failure — the strap sliding off skin mid-build — the instant it happens.

demo.program:
print("Dual-band: fabric + metal plate (contact survives wrist flex)")
print("Snap LED: green blink = path intact | dark = contact broken")
print("Catches the #1 real-world failure: strap sliding off skin mid-build.")

title: Signature Setup Ritual Card
description: Every Signature mat ships with a setup ritual card: strap on bare skin, snap cord to common point, mat snap to common point, tester green, parts in zones, humidity check. The card lives in a sleeve on the mat's edge, and builders initial and date it per session — the card becomes a log proving every build was ESD-safe. Five checks, thirty seconds, documented.

          "tester GREEN", "parts in printed zones"]
for i, s in enumerate(ritual, 1):

title: Signature Humidity Gauge Slot
description: Because dry air is the enemy, the Signature mat has a slot on its top edge holding a small analog hygrometer. The ritual card says: below 30 percent relative humidity, run the humidifier before touching parts; 40 to 50 percent is the target band. It makes the invisible visible — builders stop guessing whether the air is dry enough to matter and just read the gauge.

print("Hygrometer slot on mat edge:")
print("  <30% RH: humidifier ON before touching parts")
print("  40-50% RH: target band")
print("  The invisible (dry air) becomes a number you read.")

title: Signature CPU-First Zone Protocol
description: The Signature protocol handles the CPU before anything else, in its printed center zone: strap verified, board box opened on the mat, CPU seated by its edges, cooler mounted — all before RAM, GPU, or drives come out of their bags. The most sensitive part gets the freshest strap, the driest hands, and full attention. Everything after is lower risk and lower stress.

order = ["CPU (center zone, first)", "RAM (left zone)", "M.2 drives",
         "GPU (rest zone)", "cabling + fans"]
for i, s in enumerate(order, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {s}")
print("Most sensitive part first, on the freshest strap.")

t: Signature GPU Rest Zone With Edge Cradle
title: Signature GPU Rest Zone With Edge Cradle
description: The GPU rest zone has a printed outline plus a low silicone cradle that holds the card on its edge — bracket down, fans up — so the card never lies flat on its backplate collecting static from the bench. The cradle is dissipative silicone, bonded to the zone. Cards rest safely between power-cable routing steps instead of balancing on the case edge.

t: Signature Tool Zone: Keeping Metal Tools Drained
title: Signature Tool Zone: Keeping Metal Tools Drained
description: Screwdrivers and tweezers rest in the printed tool zone at the mat's top edge, on the dissipative surface and drained like everything else. A charged tool touching a board is a discharge path, so tools live on the mat, not on the bare bench. The zone is sized for a driver, tweezers, and the tray's edge — the whole active kit inside the protected area.

t: Signature Strap Cord Routing: The Over-Shoulder Path
title: Signature Strap Cord Routing: The Over-Shoulder Path
description: The Signature method routes the coiled strap cord up over the shoulder to the common point behind the bench, instead of across the work area. Cords across the bench snag GPUs and drag across boards; the over-shoulder path keeps the cord off the mat entirely while giving full arm reach. It is a small routing choice that removes the most annoying failure of strap cords.

demo.program:
print("Cord path: wrist -> up over shoulder -> common point behind bench")
print("NOT across the mat (snags GPUs, drags across boards).")
print("Full arm reach, zero cord interference with parts.")

t: Signature vs Standard Mat: The Zone Discipline Test
title: Signature vs Standard Mat: The Zone Discipline Test
description: On a plain mat, parts drift into piles and tools wander onto bare bench — the protection is there but the discipline is on you. On the Ground-Grid mat, every part has a printed home, so disorder is visible instantly: a RAM stick outside its zone looks wrong. In practice the printed zones keep benches organized through long builds where plain mats degrade into clutter by hour two.

print("Plain mat: protection present, discipline entirely on the builder")
print("Ground-Grid mat: every part has a printed home; disorder is visible")
print("Long builds: plain mat -> clutter by hour 2; zoned mat -> stays mapped")

t: Signature Mat Cleaning and Zone Longevity
title: Signature Mat Cleaning and Zone Longevity
description: The printed zones are under a clear dissipative overcoat, so alcohol wipes and damp cloths clean them without erasing the grid. The same banned list applies — no silicone dressings, no harsh solvents. Zone traces are in the underlayer and cannot be scrubbed away. Re-test resistivity yearly; the mat retires when any zone reads above 10^9 ohms per square.

demo.program:
print("Zones printed UNDER a clear dissipative overcoat: wipe-safe.")
print("Banned: silicone dressings, harsh solvents (coat the dissipative layer).")
print("Retire when any zone tests >1e9 ohm/sq (yearly check).")

t: Signature Winter Protocol: Dry-Air Build Rules
title: Signature Winter Protocol: Dry-Air Build Rules
description: Winter air below 30 percent humidity is peak ESD season. The Signature winter protocol: humidifier on an hour before the build, gauge reading 40 percent plus before parts leave bags, strap re-tested mid-session, and no walking across carpet with parts — sit, stay, build. The mat's hygrometer slot makes the protocol enforceable instead of aspirational.

print("Winter (RH <30%): humidifier on 1h before, gauge >=40% before unbagging,")
print("re-test strap mid-session, no carpet walks with parts.")
print("The gauge makes it a rule, not a suggestion.")

title: Signature Teardown Zones in Reverse
description: For teardowns the zones run in reverse: GPU lands in the rest zone as it comes out, RAM in the left zone, CPU last in the center zone — each part parked in its printed home the moment it leaves the machine. The mat becomes a labeled map of the disassembly, and reassembly is the zones played forward. Combined with the Hex-Zone screw tray, the whole teardown is mapped in two objects.

demo.program:
print("Teardown order -> zone: GPU->rest zone, RAM->left zone, CPU->center zone (last)")
print("Mat + Hex-Zone screw tray = the entire disassembly mapped in two objects.")
